extracted.intended_audience: general readers and policymakers interested in the French Revolution and principles of government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting standards and criteria used in a political-essay style evaluation of governments, revolutions, and public measures (taxation, confiscation, currency, judiciary, and regime form). Useful for judging whether state actions were necessary, proportionate, and salutary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral outrage at confiscation of persons and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A free man ought to feel 'indignation and horror' at the seizure and confiscation of persons and their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts that those who do not express such emotions 'do not deserve the name of a free man', implying moral opprobrium is a valid immediate test of the justice of mass expropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture only for crimes or hostile acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscation of property should be justified by the vanquished being 'composed of traitors who had borne arms, or otherwise had acted with hostility' — i.e., property forfeiture must be linked to individual crimes or hostile conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Romans tried to justify confiscations by labeling the vanquished as traitors; the text criticizes arbitrary confiscation absent such justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of measures (fiscal necessity test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary measures (confiscation, seizure) must be demonstrably necessary to preserve the existence of the state; if moderate, general taxation would suffice, seizure is unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asks whether the finances were so wretched that 'no other resource but rapine remained' and points to Necker's budget showing a relatively small deficit that could have been covered by proportionate contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of confiscation to actual fiscal deficit
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount confiscated must bear a reasonable relation to the legitimate fiscal shortfall (e.g., five million confiscated vs a deficit of £2,200,000 is disproportionate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if some resources were illusory, the author argues a need of £2,200,000 would not justify confiscations to the amount of five millions; proportionality is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for moderate, general, and proportioned assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A moderate and proportioned assessment levied upon all citizens without distinction is the proper remedy for public deficits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text favors an equal imposition across orders rather than partial or cruel confiscation targeted at particular groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify claims of privilege and actual contributions before punitive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume clergy or nobility contributed nothing; check indirect taxes, capitation, land-taxes, and other charges—actual fiscal history matters before punitive confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author documents the various taxes nobles and clergy did pay (excise on consumables, customs duties, capitation, twentieth penny, gifts, redemptions), arguing those facts undermine facile justifications for sweeping confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept voluntary or negotiated contributions when advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers by groups (e.g., clergy offering contributions) that would benefit public creditors should be accepted rather than ignored for ulterior political ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The archbishop of Aix's extravagant offer should not have been rejected; rejection suggests the motive was to destroy the church and create new landed interests, not to serve the state's creditors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic prudence in disposing of large landed property
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden mass sale of huge landed property will depress land values and harm the broader economy; disposal must consider market effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting an 'unwieldy mass' of church and crown lands simultaneously into market would depress value, divert circulating money from trade to land, and reduce the intended profits of confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating excessive new paper currency based on dubious security
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing a new paper currency founded on an eventual sale of lands (church lands) and making circulation compulsory is an outrage on credit, property, and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes creating a 3% new debt and issuing paper as security for the state's operations and to satisfy banks, calling it a combination of bankruptcy and tyranny; compulsory circulation forces the populace to support the scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abolish independent judicature to centralize power
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolishing independent courts severs the link between crown and public justice and brings justice under dictatorial control; preserve judicial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While parliaments had faults, their abolition removes a check that could allow people to 'resort to them and rally under the standard of their ancient laws.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and settlement terms must not create de facto gifts or predatory tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale terms (e.g., long deferred payments, partial up-front payment) that allow purchasers 'without money' to take possession are effectively gifts and encourage exploitation of tenants and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting twelve years to pay the rest and taking only a portion up front lets philosophic purchasers be 'put instantly into possession' and stimulates extortion from peasants and waste of materials to meet demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid binding the nation in a single guilty interest in the spoil
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures that make the existence of the new regime dependent on shared interest in plunder (paper currency, compulsory participation) force nationwide complicity and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spoil of the church becomes 'the vital principle' and 'the sole security' for the power of the new authorities; they bind individuals into a common guilty stake by compulsory paper circulation and shares in the spoil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population growth as a standard of government health
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of a country's population—growth and flourishing numbers—is a reliable indicator that the government is not very mischievous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites various estimates of French population and argues that significant population and its increase argues against the notion that monarchy wholly destroyed prosperity; population flourishing weighs in favor of a government's basic competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth and flourishing arts/manufactures/science/agriculture as standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A government's effects on wealth, arts, manufactures, science, and agriculture are key standards by which to judge whether it is protecting or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that no country where population flourishes and industry prospers can be under a very mischievous government; lists indicators such as manufactures, science, agriculture, and the human condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against substitution of one despotism for another
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of the old government does not justify replacing it with a despotism of the multitude or a new oligarchy; reform should be preferred when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that those who blacken the old government then argue opponents of their abuses must be supporters of the old tyranny; there exists a third option—mixed government—and wholesale destruction produces greater evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's risk of majority oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute democracy tends to allow a majority to exercise cruel oppression over minorities; individual sufferers are worse placed under popular persecution than under a single cruel prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Aristotle and examples, the author argues that in democracies, majorities can perpetrate persecutions 'with much greater fury' and leave victims 'deserted by mankind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mixed or tempered government
rubrics_metrics.description: A monarchy directed by laws and balanced by hereditary wealth/dignity, with suitable organs for popular reason and feeling, is preferable to extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolingbroke's observation is cited: you can better ingraft republican elements upon a monarchy than monarchy upon a republic; the author endorses a mixed constitution as historically and speculatively sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge institutions by sorting good from evil rather than wholesale condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing institutions, one should 'sort out the good from the evil' rather than become satirists and condemn entire systems; reforms are legitimate without destroying the whole fabric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises steady, independent minds to judge human institutions as they judge human characters—separating virtues from vices—rather than rushing to destructive extremes.
